Action Plan:
1. Suspected acute infectious gastroenteritis: advise strict oral re-hydration (water, oral rehydration salts) and light diet as tolerated. 
2. Safety-netting: monitor for red-flag symptoms (fever ≥38 °C, bloody stool or vomit, severe persistent abdominal pain, signs of dehydration). Seek same-day in-person GP or ED review if these occur or if symptoms worsen/continue >48–72 h. 
3. Time off work: remain at home until 48 h symptom-free to reduce possible contagion. 
4. Medication advice: antibiotics not indicated at present; continue regular asthma inhaler as needed.  
5. Follow-up: schedule routine GP appointment if diarrhoea persists >1 week, recurs, or for discussion of family bowel-cancer risk and screening options. 
6. Education provided on likely viral/food-borne etiology, hydration, and when to seek help; patient verbalised understanding. 
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: 3-day history of watery diarrhoea with central abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting.  
• History of presenting illness:  
  – Onset 3 days ago; frequency every ~10 min; no blood noted.  
  – Abdominal pain peri-umbilical, mild-to-moderate, eased after bowel motion; mild nausea; audible borborygmi.  
  – Vomited once this morning after eating fruit; no haematemesis on closer recall.  
  – No definite fever (only mild sweating); limiting oral intake; may be under-hydrated.  
  – No chest pain; baseline mild dyspnoea related to asthma only.  
• Past medical history: Asthma.  
• Medications: inhaler (brand recently changed) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: NKDA.  
• Family history: Father died of colorectal cancer at ~58 y (10 y ago).  
• Social history: Currently off work and staying near a toilet; other social factors not discussed.

Objective:
(Remote consult – no vitals taken)  
• Patient-reported mild central abdominal tenderness on self-palpation; no peritonism described.  
• No visible blood in stool or vomit reported.  
• No respiratory distress, chest pain, or other systemic red-flags reported.  
• No investigations performed during consult.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute diarrhoea / Gastroenteritis  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute infectious gastroenteritis, likely viral (DDx item: “Acute infectious gastroenteritis – likely viral”, High).  
   – Differential diagnosis:  
     • Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Medium) – less likely absent fever/ blood.  
     • IBS/post-infectious functional diarrhoea (Low-Medium) – onset too acute.  
     • Inflammatory bowel disease (Low).  
     • Colorectal carcinoma (Low) – acute course atypical but consider given family history.  
   – Investigations planned: None immediately; consider stool culture / inflammatory markers if symptoms persist >1 week or worsen.  
   – Treatment: Oral rehydration; dietary advice; avoid antibiotics unless red-flags develop.  
   – Referral: None now; GP review if no improvement in 48–72 h or earlier if red-flags.

2. Family history of colorectal cancer / Patient anxiety  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Elevated colorectal cancer concern due to first-degree relative.  
   – Differential diagnosis: n/a (risk factor rather than current illness).  
   – Investigations planned: Discuss age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening (FIT test/colonoscopy) with GP once acute illness resolves.  
   – Treatment: Education and reassurance; address anxiety.  
   – Referral: Routine GP for screening discussion.

3. Chronic asthma management  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Stable asthma; no acute exacerbation.  
   – Differential diagnosis: n/a.  
   – Investigations planned: None today.  
   – Treatment: Continue current inhaler; ensure adequate supply; review technique/brand suitability with GP if issues.  
   – Referral: None today.

Quality checks:
• Missing but expected: objective vitals (temperature, HR, BP), baseline weight/BMI, smoking/alcohol status, full medication list, past surgical history.  
• Internal conflicts:  
  – Age/DOB discrepancy (patient first stated born 1992, then age 48 implies DOB ~1975) – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor inaudible segments but clinical content intact.
